activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Sorting by color means putting all the things that are the same color together in one group.
story:
Lily ran into the playroom. Blocks were everywhere! Red blocks. Blue blocks. Yellow blocks. Green blocks. What a mess.

"Clean-up time!" said Ms. Bouchard. "Let's sort by color," said Cora. "That means all the same color blocks go together in one group."

Lily grabbed a red block. She put it in the red pile. Thunk! She grabbed another red block. Thunk! Soon the red pile was big and tall. Then she made a blue pile. Then a yellow pile. Cora made a green pile.

Lily looked at the red pile. Wait! One block was hiding in the wrong pile. It was blue! Lily picked it up. She walked it over to the blue pile. Thunk! Now every block sat with blocks just like it.

Cora clapped her hands. "All sorted!" she said. Cash held up a green block and grinned. "Look! Green pile wins. It's the tallest!"

Then Lily heard a quiet flutter by the window. A little bird spread one wing, then the other. It pecked at a yellow block on the sill. "The bird likes yellow too!" said Lily, and she waved hello.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: A librarian is a person who works at the library and helps people find books.
story:
Kinsley rode the bus with her mom. They were going to the big library. Today Kinsley would get her very first library card.

At the library, Kinsley wanted a book about trucks. She looked and looked. She saw books about cats. She saw books about the sea. But no trucks. Where could they be?

Then she saw a woman at a desk. Books were stacked all around her. Kinsley asked, "Do you work here?"

"Yes, I do," the woman said. "I am the librarian. I help people find books."

"Can you help me find truck books?" asked Kinsley.

The librarian walked to a shelf. "Here they are." There were so many trucks!

Kinsley picked a big red one. She shut the book under her arm. She held her new card up high.

On the bus home, she whispered, "I found it all by asking."

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Pulling the zipper tab down opens your coat.
story:
Nova was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. Grandma held up Nova's thick red coat.

"Can you put it on by yourself?" Grandma asked.

Nova pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. The coat was on! But the coat was open. Cold air came in at her tummy.

Nova pulled the little zipper tab up. Zzzzzip! The coat closed. Nova was warm now.

Nova and Grandma went out to the yard. There was a big puddle by the gate. Nova stomped in it. Splash! Her boots got wet and shiny.

Then Nova ran and ran. She ran to the fence and back. Now she was hot. Too hot! Sweat ran down her back.

Nova pulled the zipper tab down. Zzzzip! The coat opened. Cool air came in. Nova felt better.

"You did that all by yourself," said Grandma. "Yes I did," said Nova. "Down makes it open."

They walked to the gate. Nova pulled the tab up again. The coat closed and she was warm. She pulled it down. The coat opened and she was cool. Up and down, up and down.

"Time to come in, little one," said Grandma. Nova held her hand. They stepped over the puddle together.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: If you get lost in a store, tell a store worker you can't find your grown-up.
story:
Brooklyn went to the store with Mom. First they got bread. Then they got apples. Then they got milk. The milk case was cold. "Brrr," said Brooklyn. "My hands feel cold." The bread shelf was near a warm oven. A worker pulled hot rolls out with big gloves. Brooklyn stayed back and watched.

Brooklyn wanted to see the toy aisle. She looked and looked. Then she turned around. Mom was not there. Brooklyn could not see Mom anywhere. Where did Mom go?

Brooklyn remembered something. She walked to the front of the store. A worker in a red vest stood by the checkout. "I can't find my grown-up," said Brooklyn. "Can you help me?" The worker smiled. She used the big speaker. Soon Mom came running. "There you are!" said Mom. She gave Brooklyn a big warm hug. The worker put the bread in the bag. Brooklyn held Mom's hand all the way home.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: A toy dog is a toy, not an animal, because it is not alive.
story:
Zoey sat on the playroom floor. "Let's make piles," said Ms. Holloway. "One pile for animals. One pile for toys. One pile for food." Zoey picked up a toy apple. It went in the food pile. Then she found a toy cat with soft fur. She threw it, and it did not run away. It just sat where it fell.

Zoey held a toy dog. "Woof," she said. She put it in the animal pile. Then she stopped. The toy dog did not wag its tail. It did not blink. "It is not alive," said Cassius, sitting next to her. Zoey tapped the toy dog. It stayed very still. She picked it up. She put it in the toy pile instead.

"Good sorting, Zoey," said Ms. Holloway. Ayoub clapped his hands. Zoey smiled and patted the toy dog on its soft head.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Morning is the part of the day when we wake up and eat breakfast.
story:
Lucy made a card at school. It said "Good Morning" on it. She wanted to give it to her friend Neriah. But where was Neriah?

"Not here now," said Ms. Santos. "She will come tomorrow."

Tomorrow. Lucy tapped her foot. When was tomorrow? Yesterday they had painted together. Today Neriah was not at school. So tomorrow must be the next day.

The next morning, Lucy woke up. She peeked out of her room. The family was at the table eating breakfast. Morning was here! It was the part of the day when they woke up and ate. So today had come.

"Good morning!" Lucy said.

At school, Lucy held her card tight. The door opened. Neriah peeked in.

"I came today!" said Neriah.

Lucy ran to her. "A card for you. Good morning, Neriah!"

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Hold a grown-up's hand when you cross the street.
story:
Samuel was drawing at his desk. He made a big red ball. Then he made a messy blue sky. His crayons rolled under the desk. He had to reach far to get them.

"Time for the park," said Dad. Samuel ran to the door. He could see the swings across the road. The swings looked fun. Samuel wanted to run. He stopped at the curb and waited.

"Hold a grown-up's hand when you cross the street," Dad said. Samuel held Dad's big hand tight. They looked left. They looked right. They walked across together. Then Samuel let go and ran to the swings. Rosa was there too. "I held my dad's hand all the way," Samuel said. Rosa smiled and pushed the swing for him. "Higher, please!" Samuel said. His shoes touched the sky, almost.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: On a clear, sunny day, the sky looks blue.
story:
Willow sat at Grandma's big chair. She had a long piece of paper and a box of crayons. She wanted to draw a picture for Grandma. It would be the garden and the sky.

Willow drew red flowers. She drew yellow flowers. She drew green grass, so green and soft. Then she picked up a gray crayon. "The sky is gray," she said. She made one gray line.

Grandma looked out the window. "What a sunny day," she said. Willow looked too. The sun was bright and warm on her face. The sky was not gray at all. The sky was blue! Willow put the gray crayon back. She took the blue crayon. She filled the whole top of her page with blue.

"Look, Grandma!" said Willow. Grandma held the picture up to the window. The blue on the paper met the blue in the sky. "It matches," said Grandma. Willow smiled and drew one yellow sun.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A big circle and a tiny circle are both circles, because size does not change a shape.
story:
Kayden's class was having a shape hunt. Mr. Mehta gave each child a card. Kayden's card had a circle on it. So did Mohamed's card.

"I will find the big circle," said Mohamed. He ran to the wall clock. "Look! The clock is a circle."

Kayden looked down at his shirt. He saw a tiny button. He held it up. "My button is a circle too," he said.

Mohamed shook his head. "No way. Your button is too small. The clock is a circle."

Mr. Mehta came over. He was calm and kind. He put the button near the clock. "Put them side by side," he said.

Kayden looked at the big clock. He looked at his tiny button. He turned the button around. He traced it with his finger. Round and round it went. Round and round the clock went too.

"Both are circles!" said Kayden. "Big circle, small circle, both circles."

Mohamed traced the button too. "Both circles," he said. He smiled.

Then the boys counted their circles. One clock. Two buttons. Three stickers on the door. Kayden found a cookie in his lunch box at snack time. "The cookie is a circle too," he said. It was a cool find.

Mr. Mehta laughed. "Good hunting, boys," he said. Kayden put his button back on his shirt. He would remember this day.

"One circle," said Mohamed.

"Two circles," said Kayden.

"All circles," they said together.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: On a traffic light, red means stop and green means go.
story:
Ethan was playing cars in the playroom. Angel was there too. They had lots of shiny cars. Ethan wanted his cars to be magic.

"I know," said Ethan. "Let's make a road!" He put down a yellow scarf. It looked like a big sunny road. Angel put down a blue scarf next to it. Now the road was long.

Then Lily-Rose held up a green card. "Green means go!" she said. Ethan pushed his little red car fast, fast, fast. It zoomed down the scarves. Then Lily-Rose held up a red card. "Red means stop," she said. Ethan stopped his car. It stopped right away, like magic!

Angel smiled. She drove a yellow truck to the end of the road. There sat a stuffed bunny. The bunny held a paper flower. "Truck, take the flower to the bunny!" said Ethan. Lily-Rose held up the green card. The truck went. She held up the red card. The truck stopped.

The cars stopped and went all morning. Stop, go, stop, go. Then Ethan's dad came to the door. "Time to go home, Ethan." Ethan picked up his red car. "Can we play again tomorrow?" he asked. His dad smiled and said, "Yes, we can." Ethan waved the little car at his friends. "Beep beep," said the car.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: Hugging the ball to your chest helps you hold on to it after you catch it.
story:
Mia stood on the big grass field. Mr. Kelly put a hoop on the ground. He gave her a small red beanbag. Mia threw it. It missed. It landed in the messy grass.

"Try again," said Mr. Kelly. Mia counted, "One, two, three." She swung her arm back. She threw it soft and slow. The beanbag went up. Then it went down. It fell right into the hoop. "I did it!" said Mia. Lilith clapped. Cynthia clapped too.

Then Mr. Kelly rolled a big ball to Mia. The ball hit her hands. It bounced out. It bounced away. "Oh no," said Mia. Mr. Kelly rolled it again. The ball hit her hands. It bounced out again.

Then Mia had an idea. She waited with her arms open. The ball came. She caught it. Then she hugged it to her chest. The ball did not bounce out. It stayed right there. "One, two, three, I got it," said Mia. Mr. Kelly rolled it again, faster this time. Mia caught it and hugged it tight. The ball stayed.

Lilith ran over. "Can I try?" she asked. Mia opened her arms wide and smiled.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Christmas, many families decorate a tree.
story:
Brooklyn ran to the living room. The Christmas tree stood tall and green. "We decorate a tree at Christmas," said Grandma.

A big box sat on the floor. It was full of ornaments. Brooklyn picked up a shiny red ball. She hung it on one branch. Then she hung a snowman there too. Then a little drum. Soon one branch was full.

"Look, Mama!" said Brooklyn. "My branch is so pretty."

Maci, her cousin, came close. "The tree is empty on top," Maci said. "Only one branch has ornaments."

Brooklyn looked up. Maci was right. She took a golden star from the box. She hung it high on another branch. Then a bell. Then a silver bird. Her hands reached out, one branch at a time.

Grandma plugged in the lights. Brooklyn stood back with Maci. The whole tree danced with tiny lights.

"Now it is a dream tree," said Brooklyn. Maci laughed and held her hand.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a rainy day, a raincoat helps keep your body dry.
story:
Declan ran to the window. "Rain!" he shouted. Big drops hit the glass. Plip, plip, plip.

"I want to splash in puddles!" said Declan. He ran to the door. He opened it fast. He ran straight out into the yard.

The rain fell on his head. The rain fell on his shirt. It was cold and wet. Declan was wet all over. He ran back inside fast.

His mom held up a red coat. "Your raincoat," she said. "Put it on." Declan pushed his arms in. He zipped it up. He pulled the hood on too.

Then he ran back out. The rain fell on the hood. Plip, plip. The rain fell on the coat. Plip, plip. But Declan stayed dry under it. Not wet at all!

He touched his sleeve. The rain sat on top. It did not go through. "Dry!" he yelled. He jumped in a big puddle. The water went splash.

Maci came by in her yellow boots. "Look at all that rain!" she said. "My coat keeps me dry too!" They stomped and stomped. Two dry kids, two big puddles, one happy rainy day.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: A book return slot is a place to drop off books when bringing them back to the library.
story:
Olivia got a small blue card. It had her name on it. "Your first library card," said Grandpa. "Now you can touch a book, take it home, and keep it a while."

They went to the library. Grandpa helped her pick a book about ducks. "This one," said Olivia. She held it tight all the way home.

At home, Olivia read the duck book many times. She read it to her teddy bear. She read it to Grandpa. Then Grandpa said, "Time to take it back. But we will get a new book too."

At the library there was a little hole in the wall. "That is the book return slot," said Grandpa. "A book return slot is a place to drop off books when bringing them back to the library." Olivia held the duck book. She did not want to let it go.

"I will miss it," said Olivia. "You can pick a new one right away," said Grandpa. Olivia held the book up to the slot. She waved to the ducks. "Bye bye, ducks," she said. Then she dropped the book in. It slid down, down, down. It was gone.

Olivia looked at the slot. The book had gone in, and now the slot was empty. She had put it in, and it had gone away. She jumped a little jump. "I did that!" she said.

Then she ran to the shelf. She touched the covers, one by one. "This one," said Olivia. It was a book about a loud, bumpy truck.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A referee watches the game and makes sure players follow the rules.
story:
Anna sat on the big couch in the living room. Mama was beside her. Greyson and Bruno sat on the floor. They were all watching the big game on TV.

"Who is that man?" Anna asked. He wore a striped shirt. He kept running and looking at the players.

"That is the referee," said Mama. "The referee watches the game and makes sure the players follow the rules."

One player grabbed the ball with his hands. The referee blew his whistle. He pointed his finger. The player looked sad and let go of the ball.

"He saw it!" said Bruno.

"Yes," said Anna. "The referee watches everything."

Anna stayed awake until the end of the game. The referee blew his whistle one more time. The game was over. Mama gave Anna a warm hug. Then Anna looked at the picture of a referee she drew in her book, and smiled.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown.
story:
Ezra went to the library with his dad. He wanted a book about rocket ships. The library had big gray shelves and soft carpets. Ezra marched down the aisle. He saw a book with a red rocket on it. "This one!" he said.

Callan was there too. "Let's play rocket ship," said Callan. They stood by the carpet squares. Callan began to count. "Ten, nine, eight, seven." Ezra listened. The numbers went down, one by one. "Six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Both boys jumped up high. A girl named Agathe clapped. "That's a countdown," she said. "You count backward from ten down to one."

Ezra wanted to try. He took a deep breath. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" He jumped so high his socks almost flew off. Ms. Leblanc, the librarian, smiled. Ezra held his rocket book tight. "Ten, nine, eight," he whispered all the way home.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Two people can feel differently about the same thing.
story:
Isaiah ran to the playground. His brown shoes went clip, clip on the path. He was excited to see the big drum.

Ms. Okonkwo had put the drum by the sandbox. Isaiah hit it once. Boom! He hit it again. Boom, boom! He laughed. "One boom, two booms, three booms," he counted.

Then Lilith came near. She put her hands over her ears. "Too loud," she said. Her face looked scared. Isaiah stopped his hands. He felt sad that his friend felt scared.

But Oakleigh ran over. She was smiling big. "I love the drum!" she said. She hit it too. Boom! Isaiah looked at Lilith. He looked at Oakleigh. Same drum. One friend was happy. One friend was scared.

"Ms. Okonkwo," said Isaiah, "can Lilith and I play something quiet?"

"Yes," said Ms. Okonkwo. "The sandbox is a quiet spot."

Isaiah and Lilith dug in the brown sand. One scoop, two scoops, three scoops. Oakleigh kept the boom, boom, boom far away by the fence. Lilith smiled now. Isaiah was happy too.

"We can all play," said Isaiah. "Loud over there. Quiet over here." Lilith patted the sand. "This is just right."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Loud and quiet are opposites.
story:
Eloise was at school. It was naptime. The room was quiet. But Haylie had a drum. She banged it loud. The loud drum woke Martha up. Martha rubbed her eyes. She looked mad.

Mr. Swampy walked over. He sat down next to Haylie. "Loud and quiet are opposites," he said. "Can you play the other way?" Haylie thought hard. Then she tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. The tap was quiet. Martha did not wake up again. She went back to sleep.

Eloise watched the whole thing. She wanted to try too. She picked up a small drum. First she played it loud. The loud sound made Martha stir. Then Eloise played quiet, quiet, quiet. Nobody stirred. A flower on the shelf stood still. "I need the quiet drum for naptime," Eloise whispered. Tap, tap, tap.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: Rain makes puddles on the ground.
story:
Riley looked out the glass door. The sky was gray. "Rain," said Dad. Riley put on her rain boots. The rain made a tap-tap sound on the roof.

The rain stopped. Riley ran to the backyard. Vyom was there too. "Look!" said Vyom. He pointed at the ground. A big puddle sat in the grass. Riley stepped in it. Splash! Her boot went down in the water. She laughed and jumped again. Splash, splash. The puddle got smaller and smaller.

Soon the sun came out. It was sunny now. The wind started to blow. It blew Riley's hair all around. "My puddle is going," said Riley. She filled her glass of water and poured a little on the ground. A tiny puddle came back. "There you are," she said, and she jumped one more splash.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: After a visit ends, families can stay in touch with phone calls, video calls or letters.
story:
Grandpa came to stay at Maya's house for a whole week. Each morning they walked to the park together. Grandpa pushed Maya on the swing, way up high. "I can see a big white cloud," Maya called. Grandpa laughed and pushed her again.

They sat on the warm bench and shared a full bag of bread crumbs. The ducks came running. Maya dropped a crumb, and a duck gobbled it up. Then she dropped another crumb, and another duck ran over. "One crumb, one duck," said Grandpa.

One day Grandpa packed his suitcase. Maya felt sad. "I will miss you," she said. At home, Maya drew a picture of the big white cloud. Her mom helped her put it in an envelope. They walked to the mailbox together. Then Grandpa called on the phone, and Grandma waved on a video call. Maya held up her cloud picture to the screen. "I will draw you more," she said. Grandpa smiled.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: On your birthday, you turn one year older.
story:
Eliana turned four today. Her party was at the big swimming pool. Himmat and Willa came too.

First they swam in the shallow end. Eliana kicked her legs fast. Her kicks made big splashes. The water went up and came down on Willa's head. Willa laughed and wiped her eyes.

Then Mommy called them out of the pool. There was a cake on the picnic table. It had a soft, furry teddy bear sitting next to it. One little candle stood on top.

"I will blow it out," said Eliana.

"Not yet," said Mommy. "First, everyone count."

They counted the candle. "One!" said Himmat.

"I was three yesterday," said Eliana. "Today I am four."

"That's how birthdays work," said Ms. Harper, the lifeguard, smiling.

Eliana took a big breath. She blew hard. The flame went out. Smoke curled up like a little gray cloud. Everyone clapped.

Then Eliana saw something. Willa was shivering. Willa's towel was far away on the bench. Eliana ran and got it. She wrapped it around her friend.

"Thank you," said Willa.

Eliana sat close beside her. Then she ate her cake, all of it, down to the last bite.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your feet can feel things too, like soft grass under bare toes.
story: Dinner was outside tonight! Mom set the table on the grass. Luka ran to his seat. But his shoes felt tight and bumpy. "Ouch," he said. He sat down and could not wiggle his toes. Mom helped him pull off his shoes and socks. "Now your feet are safe and free," she said. Luka put his bare toes on the grass. The grass tickled! "My feet can feel it!" he laughed. "Soft grass under bare toes!" He sniffed the soup. It smelled like carrots. He heard Dad slurp, loud and silly. He saw steam rise up. He touched his warm cup with one finger. Then he tasted the soup. Yum! "My feet liked the grass," said Luka. "Can we eat out here every night?" Mom laughed. "Yes, little bare-feet boy."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cooks crack an egg's shell open to get the egg out.
story:
Milo woke up in the tent. "Eggs today!" he shouted. Dad laughed. "Yes, you can help."

At the little camp table, Milo held a big brown egg. He tapped it on the bowl. Tap, tap, knock. The shell cracked. Milo pulled the shell open. The egg slid out! "It came out!" he said. "Look, Dad, it came out!"

But a little piece of shell fell in too. It sat in the yellow egg like a tiny boat. "Oh no," said Milo. Dad gave him a spoon. Milo dipped the spoon in. He fished out the piece of shell. "Got it!"

"Ready to cook?" said Dad. Dad lit the little camp stove. Milo stood back, far from the hot pan. He watched the egg go round and flat. "It makes a circle!" said Milo. "It makes a sun shape!"

The egg went onto a plate. Milo carried the plate to the tent, low and slow, both hands holding tight. "Breakfast!" he called. Mom sat up and smiled. "For me? Thank you, Milo!"

Milo grinned. "I cracked the shell. The egg came out!"

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: An indoor cat uses a litter box as its toilet.
story:
Riley went to the park with Dad. There was a little tent there. Kittens sat in a big pen. One small kitten had white paws. It looked at Riley. "This one," said Riley. Dad said, "We can take her home today."

At home, Dad put a box on the floor. It had soft sand inside. Riley pointed at it. "What is that?" she asked. "A litter box," said Dad. "The kitten goes to the toilet in it."

Riley watched the kitten. The kitten sniffed the sand. The kitten moved her paws. Then the kitten used the box. Riley clapped. "Good kitten!" she said.

At night the kitten sang a little song. Riley gave her water. She petted her softly. "Careful," said Dad. "Her claws are sharp." Riley touched the kitten very gently. The kitten purred and purred. "Good kitten," Riley said again.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: In and out are opposites.
story: Evan was at daycare. He had a big red box. He put a toy bear in the box. He put a little car in the box. He put a shiny ball in the box. The box was his soup pot. "This is bear soup," he said. "It is hot soup!" But then Andreas ran up. Andreas took the bear out. Andreas took the car out. Andreas took the ball out too. The soup pot was empty. Evan wanted his soup back. He put the bear in again. Andreas took it out again. In, out, in, out. "Hey!" said Evan. "You take out. I put in." Ms. González smiled. "In and out are opposites," she said. Evan looked at the box. Then he had a neat idea. He turned the box upside down. All the toys stayed under it. "No more out!" said Evan. Andreas tapped the box like a drum. Boom, boom! "Now it is a drum," said Andreas. Evan laughed and tapped too.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
fact: A bright light above the dentist's chair helps the dentist see inside your mouth.
story:
Layla and her dad went to the pharmacy. The shelves were tidy and bright. "We need a new toothbrush," Dad said. "You see the dentist today."

Layla picked a small blue toothbrush. The cashier put it in a bag. Layla held the bag all the way to the dentist.

The dentist's room had a big window. Layla sat in the chair. A bright light shone down above her. Layla squeezed her eyes shut. It was too bright!

"Here," the dentist said. She gave Layla tiny sunglasses. Layla put them on. Now she could open her eyes. The light did not hurt.

"Say ahh," said the dentist. Layla opened her mouth wide. The light above the chair helped the dentist see inside. "Nice teeth," the dentist said.

Layla looked at herself in a little mirror. A girl in sunglasses, at the dentist. She laughed. "I look funny," she said.

On the way home, Layla stirred her shoe in a puddle and smiled. "Can I wear the sunglasses again tomorrow?" she asked Dad. Dad laughed and held her hand.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Heavy and light are opposites.
story:
Louis ran to the park with his mom. He wanted to build a big pile of leaves. "I will make it big," he said. Inayah was there too. She had a small purple bag.

Louis found a big rock. He pushed it. The rock did not move. He pushed again. It still did not move. "It is too heavy," said Louis. Inayah pushed too. Still no. It stayed right there.

Then Louis found a feather pillow by the blanket. He picked it up. Up it went, so easy! "This is light," he said. "The rock is heavy, and the pillow is light," said Inayah. "Heavy and light are opposites."

Louis put the pillow on the grass. He put light leaves on top. The pile grew and grew. He jumped in. The leaves flew up. "Soft fall," said Louis. His mom clapped. "Time for a cold drink," she said. Louis smiled and gave Inayah the first cup.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Learning to zip your own coat takes practice.
story:
Charlie was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. Charlie wanted to play in the snow.

"Put on your coat," said Grandma. Charlie tried to zip it up. The zipper did not move. She tried again. Still no zip. Charlie felt like crying a little.

"You can get it," said Grandma. "Try it again." Charlie put the zipper in the little slot. She pulled it up slowly. Zip! It worked! Charlie smiled big.

She put on her striped boots too. Then she and Grandma went outside. Charlie zipped her coat all by herself again at the door. The snow was soft and white.

"I did it, Grandma!" said Charlie. Grandma clapped her hands.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Written music uses marks called notes to show which sounds to play.
story:
Hannah went to the music room at the community center. Mr. Wright had a drum there. He also had a big paper with dots and lines on it.

"What are the dots?" Hannah asked.

"Those are notes," said Mr. Wright. "Written music uses notes to show which sounds to play." Hannah tapped a note. She made a boom on the drum. She tapped a short note and made a quick boom. She tapped a big dot and made a long, loud boom. One dot made one sound. She tapped two dots fast. Boom, boom!

Colter came in. "Play with me," said Hannah. He tapped the notes. She played his sounds. He tapped high, she played high. He tapped low, she played low.

Mr. Wright smiled. "You two can play at the party on Friday."

"I know a song now," said Hannah. She tapped one note and waited. Colter hit the drum. Boom. Hannah laughed and clapped her hands.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: The spot where you got a shot can feel sore for a little while afterward.
story:
Joshua ran into the doctor's office. He saw a big fish tank. "Look, Mom, a blue fish!" he said. A sign on the wall said "Shots Today." Joshua held his mom's hand tight. The nurse called his name.

"Time for your shot," the nurse said. Joshua sat very still. The nurse touched his arm. Then, pop! The shot was done. "That was fast!" said Joshua. The nurse gave him a crunchy cracker. Joshua munched it all up.

In the car, Joshua bumped his arm on his seat. "Ow!" he said. "My arm hurts." Mom looked at him. "The spot where you got your shot can feel sore for a little while," she said. Joshua rubbed the spot gently. Then he squeezed his toy dinosaur. "You can be sore too," he told the dinosaur. "It will feel better soon."

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'hello' when you meet someone is a friendly way to greet them.
story:
Maeva was at school. It was drawing time. She wanted the red color. Joelle had the red color.

Maeva hid behind the big paper shelf. She peeked out at Joelle. She did not say anything. Joelle did not look up. Joelle kept drawing her cat.

Mr. Shin walked over. "Say hello," he said to Maeva, softly. Maeva peeked out again. "Hello, Joelle," she said. Joelle looked up and smiled. "Hello, Maeva!"

"Please can I have the red color?" asked Maeva. "Yes, here you go," said Joelle. "Thank you," said Maeva.

Maeva began to draw. Her hand bumped the cup. Dirty water spilled on the table. "Sorry," said Maeva. "It is okay. I will help," said Joelle. They wiped the table together.

Hello, hello, hello. Maeva said it again at play time, to Maxime too. Everyone smiled back. Then Maeva sat down and drew a big red flower. "Hello, flower," she whispered.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In basketball, a team scores by getting the ball through the hoop.
story:
Charlie had a red ball. His dad put a hoop on the fence. "You score when the ball goes through the hoop," said Dad. Charlie threw the ball. It hit the fence. It did not go through. "Oh no," said Charlie.

His friend Quentin came to play. Quentin threw the ball too. It went over the hoop. It did not go through. "The ball keeps missing!" said Quentin. Charlie made a mad face. Then he stuck out his tongue at the ball. "Bad ball," he said, and he laughed.

They practiced and practiced. Charlie threw the ball up, up, up. It went through the hoop. It dropped down. "It went in! We scored!" said Charlie. Quentin clapped his hands. "My turn, my turn!" said Quentin. He ran to get the ball.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: Taking slow, deep breaths can help you feel calmer when you are scared.
story:
Avery sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her mama held her hand. On the wall was a picture of a yellow duck. Avery liked the duck. But her tummy felt jumpy.

"The nurse will come soon," said Mama. Avery did not want a shot. She wanted to go home. She looked at the duck some more. Her legs swung fast under the chair.

The nurse came in with a small tray. Avery hid her face on Mama's shoulder. "I am scared," she said. "Let's try something," said Mama. "Breathe in slow, like you are smelling a flower." Avery sniffed a big, slow breath in. "Now blow out slow, like you are blowing out a candle." Avery blew out, slow and long.

They did it again. Sniff the flower. Blow the candle. One more time. Avery's shoulders came down. Her tummy felt less jumpy. "I feel better," she said. The nurse said, "Ready?" Avery held still and kept breathing slow. The shot was quick, like a tiny pinch. Then it was done.

Avery got a bright bandage with stars on it. On the road home, she practiced her slow breaths again. Sniff the flower. Blow the candle. "Look, Mama," she said. "I can do it all by myself."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: An apron or an old shirt keeps paint off your clothes.
story:
Peyton ran into the art studio. She wore her favorite shirt. It was blue with a little pig on it.

"Time to paint," said Mr. Hughes. "Put on your aprons."

Abygael put on her apron. It was loose and big. Peyton wanted to paint a pig, so she began right away.

The brush dripped. Red paint fell on her blue shirt. Peyton looked down. Her pig was covered in red.

"Oh no," she said. "Will it come out?"

Mr. Hughes brought her an old shirt. "Wear this," he said.

Peyton put it on. It was long and loose. She dipped her brush again. Drip, drip. The paint fell on the old shirt. Her blue shirt stayed clean underneath.

"Look at that," said Abygael.

Peyton painted her pig. More drips fell. None got on her clothes.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: People say 'please' when they ask for something.
story:
Evelyn went to the store with her dad. The sky outside looked stormy. Evelyn wanted the big red apple on the shelf. It was too high up.

A boy named Bryson stood by the juice. "Give me juice!" he said. His mom shook her head. Then Bryson said, "Juice, please." His mom smiled and put the juice in the cart.

Evelyn slid her hand along the cool shelf. Then she looked up at the store man. "Apple, please," she said. The store man smiled big. He reached up and put the apple in her hand.

"Thank you," said Evelyn. "You are welcome," said the store man. Outside, the stormy sky began to clear. Evelyn held the apple all the way home. "Apple, please!" she said again, at her own house, just to hear it once more.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Fans often wear their team's colors to show which team they cheer for.
story:
Aria put on her red shirt. She loved her red shirt. Then she ran to the big field with her dad.

The game was about to start. One team wore blue shirts. The other team wore red shirts, just like Aria. A man with a big horn looked at Aria. "Yay, red team!" he said. He gave her a red flag to wave.

But Aria did not want the red team. She wanted the blue team. Lachlan was there, waving a blue flag. "Blue team is my team," he said. "I wear blue so everyone knows."

Aria looked down at her red shirt. That was why the man cheered at her! So she ran to her dad. "Can I wear my blue sweater?" she asked. Her dad pulled it from the bag. Aria put it on over the red shirt. Now she looked all blue.

The man with the horn looked again. He laughed. "Blue team too?" he said. He gave her a blue flag. A dog near the fence gave one happy bark. The crowd got loud, then quiet, then loud again, like a big ocean of voices.

Aria waved her blue flag high. "Go, blue team!" she called.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In basketball, players score by throwing the ball through a hoop.
story:
The big game was on TV. Wesley sat on the rug in the living room. Dad was there. Raavi was there too. Alexandria sat on the small chair.

A player ran with the ball. He threw it up high. It went right through the hoop! The crowd went wild.

"He threw the ball through the hoop," said Wesley. "That is how they score!"

"Can I try?" asked Wesley. Dad found a soft ball and a toy hoop. He held it up high on the wall.

Wesley threw the ball. It hit the wall and fell down. He tried again. Too far to the left. Raavi was quiet. Then Wesley stepped closer. He threw the ball up.

Swish! Through the hoop it went. The ball dropped to the floor.

"I did it!" said Wesley. "I scored!"

"Good throw," said Alexandria. She clapped her hands.

"Again," said Wesley. He picked up the ball.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, players try to get the ball into the net to score a goal.
story:
Adam sat at the big table. His friend Thalia sat next to him. Up on the wall was a big, bright screen. A soccer game was on. Adam's dad had brought a gray hat for Adam. It was a little gift for game day.

A player ran with the ball. He kicked it hard. The ball flew low. Adam held his breath. "It has to go over the net," Adam said. Thalia shook her head. "No, watch," she said.

The ball went into the net. The net moved and bulged out. The whole restaurant shouted, "Goal!" Adam clapped his hands. "The ball goes in the net," Adam said. Thalia smiled. On the screen, the player ran and jumped. Adam waved his hat in the air.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: Library books are shared with many other people, so we take care not to tear or write in them.
story: Rose went to the big library with her dad. It was dark and quiet inside. "Can I really take a book home?" she asked. "Yes, today you get your own library card," Dad said. Mr. Yilmaz made the card. It had Rose's name on it. Rose picked a book about a red triangle. She sat down and opened it. She found a crayon in her pocket. She wanted to draw a cat on the page. Then she saw small fingerprints on the paper. Other kids had read this book too. Mr. Yilmaz came over. Rose asked, "Do other people read this book?" "Many people share it, so we take care not to tear it or write in it," he said. Rose listened. She put the crayon away. She drew her cat on her own paper instead. Then she held her new card tight and checked out the triangle book all by herself. "See you soon, book," she whispered.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: When you count, you say one number word for each object and count each object only once.
story:
Amira sat at the big table in math club. Ms. Perera put down two trays of apples. "Which tray has more?" she asked.

Avi counted the red apples fast. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven!" But Amira looked closely. He had counted one apple two times. "Try again," she said. "Point at each apple once." Avi pointed carefully. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six apples, not seven.

Amira counted the green tray next. She touched each apple one time. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." She counted it two times, just to be sure. Eight was more than six. "The green apples have more!" she said in a loud, happy voice.

"Good counting," said Ms. Perera. Shanaya giggled. "Avi, your apple was tricky!"

Avi laughed too. "You silly apple," he told it. Then he tapped it once, like a drum.
